question: A 50-year-old man presents to an ophthalmologist with progressive decrease in his visual acuity over the last 6 months. He also mentions that he has become excessively sensitive to light over the same duration. Past medical history is significant for schizophrenia diagnosed in early adulthood which has been managed with an antipsychotic medication for the past 20 years. The ophthalmologist performs a slit lamp examination and notes discrete brown deposits on the corneal epithelium in both eyes. Which of the following antipsychotic drugs has this patient most likely been taking?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Progressive decrease in visual acuity" -> "Excessive sensitivity to light" -> "Brown deposits on corneal epithelium" -> "Chlorpromazine" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Progressive decrease in visual acuity" -> "Excessive sensitivity to light" -> "Brown deposits on corneal epithelium" -> "Thioridazine" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Progressive decrease in visual acuity" -> "Excessive sensitivity to light" -> "Brown deposits on corneal epithelium" -> "Clozapine" -> "Unclear association" -> 40%
CHAIN: "Progressive decrease in visual acuity" -> "Excessive sensitivity to light" -> "Brown deposits on corneal epithelium" -> "Haloperidol" -> "Unclear association" -> 30%
CHAIN: "Progressive decrease in visual acuity" -> "Excessive sensitivity to light" -> "Brown deposits on corneal epithelium" -> "Ziprasidone" -> "Unclear association" -> 30%
enhanced_information: The patient's symptoms of progressive decrease in visual acuity, excessive sensitivity to light, and brown deposits on the corneal epithelium are most strongly associated with the use of Thioridazine. This aligns with the consensus that Thioridazine can cause pigmentary retinopathy and corneal deposits, leading to visual disturbances. Chlorpromazine is also known to cause similar ocular side effects, but the association is stronger with Thioridazine. The retrieved evidence paths do not directly support the specific ocular effects of these drugs and are too broad to be relevant. Therefore, based on standard medical consensus, Thioridazine is the most likely antipsychotic drug the patient has been taking.
analysis: The patient's symptoms of progressive decrease in visual acuity, excessive sensitivity to light, and brown deposits on the corneal epithelium are indicative of ocular side effects associated with certain antipsychotic medications. Among the options provided, Thioridazine is well-documented to cause pigmentary retinopathy and corneal deposits, which can lead to visual disturbances. Chlorpromazine can also cause ocular side effects, but the specific combination of symptoms described is more strongly associated with Thioridazine. Therefore, based on standard medical knowledge and consensus, Thioridazine is the most likely antipsychotic drug the patient has been taking.
